analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal rule requiring prevailing wages on federally funded construction projects.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the Davis-Bacon prevailing wage requirement attracted only 3 cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This one-page bill would repeal the Davis-Bacon Act, the law requiring contractors on federally funded construction to pay workers the locally prevailing wage. It would also wipe out every wage requirement in other laws that points to Davis-Bacon, taking effect 30 days after passage while leaving existing contracts untouched. Contractors could then bid on federal jobs paying whatever the market allows, often less than the prevailing wage.
analysis.who_benefits: Contractors bidding on federal construction projects gain the most: they could lower their labor costs by paying below the locally prevailing wage. Taxpayers could see some savings if bids come in lower, though whether savings materialize or simply flow to contractors is contested.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal construction contractors bidding on public projects

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Davis-Bacon Act itself, ending the requirement that laborers and mechanics on federally financed or assisted construction be paid the locally prevailing wage.
Declares null and void every reference in any other law to a Davis-Bacon wage requirement, so wage floors woven into federal grant and contract programs would disappear too.
Gives contractors 30 days of notice and shields contracts already in existence or under bids outstanding on the enactment date, avoiding disruption to current projects.

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers on federally funded projects, who would earn less once the prevailing-wage floor disappeared; prevailing-wage rules set pay for various classes of laborers and mechanics on public buildings and public works, and repeal removes that floor.

drawbacks.text: The bill's direct cost falls on the very workers Davis-Bacon was written to protect: various classes of laborers and mechanics on federally financed or assisted construction who are currently guaranteed the locally prevailing wage.
Because the bill voids references to Davis-Bacon in any other law, workers on a wide range of federally assisted projects — not just direct federal construction — could lose wage protections at once.
Repeal takes effect 30 days after enactment, so workers on soon-to-bid projects would have little time before lower wage rates applied.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's gains would go to contractors in the form of lower labor costs, with any taxpayer savings uncertain and passed-through only if competitive bidding actually lowers prices. The cost is certain and direct: a wage cut for construction workers on public projects. It is a simple transfer of money from workers' paychecks to contractors' margins, with no offsetting protection for the workers affected.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve King of Iowa introduced the Davis-Bacon Repeal Act on February 22, 2019, with Reps. Gosar and Duncan joining as original cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor, which is where wage-law legislation is considered.
Three Republicans cosponsored the bill in total, and the House Education and Labor Committee never held a markup or scheduled it for a floor vote for the rest of the Congress.
The bill received no further action of any kind and died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction workers on federally funded projects are better off, because the locally prevailing wage requirement they currently work under remains in force. Contractors who wanted to pay below the prevailing wage on federal jobs gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Construction workers whose prevailing wage floor survived

for.name: Rep. Steve King
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Davis-Bacon Repeal Act and recruited two original cosponsors.

for.name: Reps. Paul Gosar and John Duncan
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; one more Republican later joined for 3 cosponsors total.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Bobby Scott (D)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the life of the Congress.

against.name: 116th Congress
against.what_they_did: The two-year session ended with the bill still in committee, ending it automatically under House rules.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; the bill's entire support — the sponsor and 3 cosponsors — was Republican, and the Democratic-controlled committee never acted on it.

industries.note: Contractors could bid on federally financed or assisted construction without paying the locally prevailing wage, cutting their labor costs directly out of workers' pay. The gain to contractors is the mirror of the loss to workers, which is why the bill's benefit is concentrated and one-sided.

Various classes of laborers and mechanics on public buildings and public works would lose the prevailing-wage floor Davis-Bacon provides, since most have no other way to capture the savings. The bill voids references in other laws too, widening the exposure.
Prevailing-wage rules keep nonunion and union contractors competing on a common pay floor on public work; repeal would let low-wage bids undercut that standard on federally funded projects.
